title: Arjuna drops his bow
hook: on the battlefield, Arjuna sinks down in despair

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ayyub, the Quran's Job, who named his harm and was still called patient. Your line was he called out. Who did you ask for help? Today the theme of suffering moves to the Bhagavad Gita, and a warrior who can't go on. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

Conch shells blow. Two armies stand facing each other on a wide field called Kurukshetra, ready. In the middle, a chariot rolls out between them, and in it stands the archer Arjuna, with his friend Krishna holding the reins. Arjuna asked for this: drive me out, let me see who I'm fighting. Krishna does. And Arjuna looks across the field and sees the faces. Not strangers. His teachers. Grandfathers. Cousins, uncles, friends. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture set inside the epic Mahabharata, begins right here, with a hero falling apart.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, READY.` → `DRIVE ME OUT. LET ME SEE.` → `HE SEES THE FACES.`

segments.voice: First, the body. The Gita doesn't make Arjuna's despair noble or tidy. It makes it physical. His limbs give way, he says, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles, his hair stands on end. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and his skin burns. He can't stand. His mind is reeling. Second, the reasons. He makes his case: what good is a kingdom won by killing the people I love? I don't want victory, or pleasures, or a throne, if this is the price. His argument is serious, and the text lets him make all of it. Third, the drop. At the end of the first chapter, Arjuna casts away his bow and arrows and sinks down on the seat of the chariot, his mind overwhelmed with grief. At the start of the second, he tells Krishna plainly, I will not fight, and falls silent. Tradition names this whole first chapter for his despair. Fourth, why it matters. Everything else in the Gita, all of Krishna's teaching, comes after this collapse, and in answer to it. Tradition says Krishna here is God, teaching his friend; some readers also hear the battle as the struggle inside any person. Either way, the conversation doesn't begin while Arjuna is pretending to be fine. It begins when he puts the bow down, sits, and admits he doesn't know what to do. The text opens its wisdom to a person in despair, not to a person who has it together.
screen: `HIS LIMBS GIVE WAY.` · `WHAT GOOD IS A KINGDOM?` · `HE CASTS AWAY THE BOW.` · `THE TEACHING BEGINS AFTER.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle into the seat, the way Arjuna sank onto his. Notice if there's one place in your life where you've been gripping the bow: holding it together, acting fine. Now admit, silently, one despair. One thing you don't know how to face, or don't want to. Say it plainly to yourself: I don't know what to do about this. Feel what the body does when you say it. Maybe a tightening, maybe a little release. You don't need an answer yet. Arjuna didn't have one either. The bell holds the time.
Gandiva, Arjuna's bow in the Gita, slips from his hand as despair overtakes him before Krishna's teaching begins. Today's word.
Your line: dropped the bow. Today, admit one despair to one person you trust, without fixing it first. Day seven hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is read and recited at home, in temples and in study groups, and its first chapter, Arjuna's despair, is heard as the opening that makes the teaching possible.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. you asked to see the enemy, and you see your teachers and cousins. your bow is in your hand. what do you do?

original.note: Sanskrit: despair, dejection; tradition names the Gita's first chapter for Arjuna's viṣāda.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bhagavad Gita is a calm book of wisdom from start to finish.
what it means: it begins with a warrior so overwhelmed he drops his bow and refuses to fight.
what a scholar hears: Gita 1.28–47 and 2.9; the first chapter traditionally titled for Arjuna's viṣāda, his despair.

notes: All Gita passages paraphrased; no translation quoted (Arnold 1885 not used because wording not verified). 1.21–23 (Arjuna asks Krishna to place the chariot between the armies), 1.26 (he sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends), 1.28–30 (limbs fail, mouth dries, trembling, hair on end, Gandiva slips, skin burns, mind reels), 1.31–35 (no desire for victory or kingdom), 1.47 (casts away bow and arrows, sits in the chariot, overwhelmed with sorrow), 2.9 ('I will not fight', falls silent). Confirm.
'Grandfathers' follows 1.26's list (fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, friends); Bhishma and Drona are named in 1.25.

Editor: replaced the garbled 'His grandfather figure' with the Gita's own list (grandfathers); 'In Hindu tradition, Krishna here is God' softened to 'tradition says'; howItsDone no longer generalizes about all Hindus; source range widened to 1.1 and 1.12 for Kurukshetra and the conch shells in the hook.
'Tradition names this whole first chapter for his despair' refers to the colophon title Arjuna-vishada-yoga; confirm.

'Some readers also hear the battle as the struggle inside any person' (an allegorical reading associated with, e.g., Gandhi) is attributed loosely; confirm it is fair alongside readings that take the battle literally.
